clue.text: I keep saying this femme fatale has no power

indicators.note: has no tells us a letter is dropped from the word the femme fatale gives

parts.note: a femme fatale is a seductive woman who ensnares men, a MANTRAP
P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: Someone keeps repeating that the seductive woman has lost her hold over them.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase chanted over and over in meditation is exactly something one keeps saying.

clue.text: My abilities sell tragic content in satire

indicators.note: being content in something means being held inside it, so the shuffled letters sit within the satire word

parts.note: a skit is a short satirical sketch

indicators.note: tragic suggests a disaster, so the four letters of sell are wrecked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of their talent for selling tragedy wrapped up in comic satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tragic' is the anagram signal, not a description of the sale; 'content in' reads as contentment but means held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's full range of competences is called their set of skills, so it names what they are able to do.

clue.text: Boatman's spirit seen in colour of president

indicators.note: seen in says one word is found sitting inside another

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour
rum is the traditional sailor's drink; Boatman is also the setter's own name

explanation.surface: The setter's drink is found in the complexion of a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is this puzzle's setter, so the clue jokes about his own tipple: the navy's rum ration.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry S. Truman was the 33rd US president, serving from 1945 to 1953.

clue.text: Revolution in USA! Try supporting last to give mouth

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so the shuffled letters come after the single letter
last to points at the final letter of the following word
a revolution overturns the order of things, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A political slogan: revolution in America, giving it a try by backing the underdog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last to give' supplies E; 'Revolution in' rearranges USA and TRY into STUARY, which goes below E.
explanation.definitionFit: A river's tidal mouth, where it widens into the sea, is called this.

clue.text: Alternatively, dressed down with a flower

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
chid is an old past tense of chide, to scold or dress down

explanation.surface: Someone is either scolded or handed a bloom as a consolation.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchids are a large family of exotic flowering plants prized for their blooms.

clue.text: Clue for Northern Ireland, taking its place

parts.note: the two-word phrase read as an instruction says take IN and turn it round, which gives NI, the abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A crossword clue is needed for Northern Ireland, filling its slot in a list.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer, read as wordplay, is the clue for NI. Its definition is 'taking its place', in the sense of each in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing things one after another, each in sequence, means each takes its place in the order.

clue.text: Kennedy famously meeting Castro in crisis — no sign of thaw?

indicators.note: something in crisis is thrown into turmoil, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: John F. Kennedy is famously known by his initials JFK

explanation.surface: JFK meeting Castro during the Cuban Missile Crisis, with no thaw in the Cold War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in crisis' rearranges JFK plus CASTRO. 'no sign of thaw' tempts toward the Cold War; it is really the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The folklore figure personifying frosty, icy weather appears exactly when there is no thawing.

clue.text: President opening Gettysburg Address with passion

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to rant is to speak loudly and passionately

explanation.surface: A president begins the Gettysburg Address with great fervour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gettysburg Address was Lincoln's, which pulls toward him; the wordplay instead takes G from 'Gettysburg'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses S. Grant, Union general in the Civil War, became the 18th US president.

clue.text: Gods here reflect the head of state on high, my fate, my beginning

indicators.note: the beginning of the word is its first letter
a reflection shows things back to front, so the whole string is read from right to left
the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: up means on high
one's lot is one's fate

explanation.surface: A grandiose statesman muses on his lofty destiny and origins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflect' reverses everything: S + UP + MY + LOT + M becomes the answer read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek mountain was the home of Zeus and the Olympian deities, so it is where the gods are.

clue.text: Perhaps Bush shredded his letters about the end of the USSR

indicators.note: about says the shuffled letters go round the next piece
shredding tears something into pieces, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of Bush, the name just given

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: President Bush destroys his correspondence about the collapse of the Soviet Union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shredded' jumbles BUSH into SHUB; 'about' wraps it round R, the end of USSR. 'Perhaps' marks Bush as an example of the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A bush is one kind of woody plant smaller than a tree, so it exemplifies the general term.

clue.text: Bottoms up! It's a reason to fill your glass

indicators.note: in a down clue, bottom-up means the letters are read upwards, i.e. backwards

explanation.surface: A toast: cheers, here is an excuse to top up your drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottoms up' looks like a drinking toast; in a down clue it reverses IT'S A.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont is something to pour into a glass.

clue.text: Constituents of Adams once produced fruit

indicators.note: Constituents of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Voters for President Adams once came up with a crop.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'produced fruit' is changed to 'fruit': 'produced' is the link verb joining wordplay to definition, and the answer is a fruit, not a produced one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small dark purple plum, used for jams and gin, is a type of fruit.

clue.text: Perhaps Reagan lost his head in office?

indicators.note: losing one's head here means the first letter is removed

parts.note: Ronald Reagan was an example of a US head of state

explanation.surface: Did Reagan lose his temper while serving in power?
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost his head' sounds like losing one's temper; it removes the first letter P.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living in a place, or a diplomat posted there, is installed and in post, so loosely in office.

clue.text: "It's important to maintain trust", Eisenhower said on diplomacy

indicators.note: said signals that the president's nickname is to be heard as spoken, its sound giving the start of the answer

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of President Dwight D. Eisenhower
tact is diplomacy, sensitivity in dealing with people

explanation.surface: Eisenhower offers a quotation about diplomacy and the importance of keeping faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'Ike on tact' out loud and it runs together as the answer: IKE heard is EYE plus the C sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking someone in the eye while talking is said to build trust, so keeping it up matters.

clue.text: One in temporary accommodation

indicators.note: in says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a tent is a temporary shelter
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: Someone living in a short-term lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a renter is one living in a home that is not permanently theirs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rents a home occupies it on a lease, which is not permanent ownership.

clue.text: Sails hauled tight on boat of Florida president

parts.note: FL is the postal abbreviation for Florida
a is an old or dialect form of of, as in man-a-war
William Howard Taft was the 27th US president

explanation.surface: A Floridian president goes sailing with the sheets trimmed hard.
explanation.definitionFit: This nautical term describes a vessel's sails trimmed in hard and pulled tight fore and aft.

clue.text: Flower seen in autumn in US, with leaf's first drop

indicators.note: drop here means remove a letter from the word for autumn

parts.note: Americans call autumn fall

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A bloom spotted in the American autumn as leaves begin to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a crossword trick: something that flows, i.e. a river. The Fal is a river in Cornwall, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is something that flows, which is the crossword sense of the clue's first word.

clue.text: See 15
President might introduce ads to create trends or reach family men?

definitions.text: President might introduce ads to create trends or reach family men?

parts.words: President might introduce ads to create trends or reach family men?
parts.note: read as a puzzle: put the word for advertisements into this president's surname after its first letter and you start a word for trends; tack it on the end and the result reads as aimed at fathers

explanation.surface: A president considers using advertising to start fashions or appeal to fathers.
explanation.walkthrough: Playful clue: put ADS into the name after F to start FADS, trends; tack ADS on the end and it reads 'for dads', aimed at family men.
explanation.definitionFit: Gerald Ford was the 38th US president, also the name of the carmaker famous for advertising.

clue.text: President losing his cool but triumphed without getting the bird

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the victory word surrounds the rest

parts.note: won means triumphed

indicators.note: losing says some letters are taken away from the president's name

parts.note: Calvin Coolidge was the 30th US president
taken as written, removed from the name

explanation.surface: A president loses his composure yet wins, though he is booed by the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing his cool' sounds like a temper; it removes COOL from COOLIDGE, leaving IDGE. 'getting the bird' suggests being jeered.
explanation.definitionFit: A wigeon is a species of dabbling duck, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Unexpectedly agile FDR becomes president

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests things turning out differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Roosevelt, who was disabled, surprisingly becomes nimble.
explanation.walkthrough: FDR (Franklin D. Roosevelt) pulls toward him as the president; his initials are only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: James A. Garfield was the 20th US president, assassinated in 1881.

clue.text: See 14
Clinton reputedly with wanton harlot says: "I have to pay?"

indicators.note: wanton means unruly or undisciplined, so the letters run wild
says means spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: I owe means I have to pay, heard as the two letters I O

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton, with a loose woman, asks whether he must pay for her services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanton' rearranges HARLOT into LOTHAR; 'I owe' spoken sounds like the letters I O.
explanation.definitionFit: A womanising seducer of women, which is what Clinton was reputed to be.

clue.text: President, one in role of a nation's leader: he does magic?

indicators.note: playing the role of means replacing, so one letter stands in for another

parts.note: Barack Obama was the 44th US president
the letter itself, taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: a word's leader is its first letter

explanation.surface: A president plays the role of a national leader, a kind of political magician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in role of' swaps I for the first A of OBAMA, giving OBIMA, then N from 'nation's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah, or obi, is Caribbean folk sorcery, and its practitioner works spells.

clue.text: Not wholly macho, overworked president

indicators.note: not wholly means only part of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A head of state who is partly macho and worked too hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Hoover was the 31st US president, in office when the Depression began.

clue.text: President: no hesitation getting on the box

indicators.note: no tells us the hesitation sound is removed from the name

parts.note: Jimmy Carter was the 39th US president
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A president appears on television without hesitating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the box' is British slang for television, which the surface suggests; here it is a cardboard container.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardboard or paper container, such as for milk or eggs, is a kind of box.

clue.text: Perhaps Lincoln led servant from the bottle

indicators.note: led means went in front, so the vehicle comes before the servant

parts.note: Lincoln is a brand of car, so it is an example
boy is an old word for a male servant

explanation.surface: Abraham Lincoln brought a servant away from drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' looks like the president; it is the car marque.
explanation.definitionFit: A large glass or plastic container, often in a protective frame, holding acids; a big bottle.

clue.text: Fool, foolishly hoaxed

indicators.note: foolishly means in a silly, disordered way, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: An idiot has been tricked, stupidly enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a blockhead with the brains of a bovine is an old insult for a stupid person.

clue.text: President laid bare?

definitions.meaning: split as ..., nothing on, i.e. naked

explanation.surface: A president is exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the name: NIX (nothing) ON, so wearing nothing. It also hints at Watergate exposing him.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Nixon led the US from 1969 until resigning over Watergate in 1974.

clue.text: Boatman caught in delicate illumination

indicators.note: caught in says the sailor is held inside the other word

parts.note: slight means delicate or slender
a tar is a sailor; Boatman is also the setter's name

explanation.surface: The setter is caught in a soft glow of light.
explanation.definitionFit: The faint glow coming from stars at night is a form of light.

clue.text: Lack of clarity in speech by president

indicators.note: in speech means spoken, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: haze is mistiness, a lack of clarity

explanation.surface: A president's address is muddled and unclear.
explanation.definitionFit: Rutherford B. Hayes was the 19th US president, elected in the disputed 1876 race.

clue.text: Start to salivate about bun (chocolate?) seen in window

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: c is short for circa, Latin for about
a roll is a bread bun
a bar is perhaps a chocolate bar, shown by the question mark

explanation.surface: Mouth starts watering at a chocolate bun displayed in a bakery window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'window' suggests a shop window; it is a computer window.
explanation.definitionFit: On screen, the vertical strip used to move through a document appears at the side of a program's window.
